title: How to Sell a Condo in Singapore (2026 Guide)
summary: Selling a condo in Singapore? Learn the process, SSD rules, costs, OTP, CPF refunds and what to calculate before accepting an offer.
body_markdown:
Last Updated on August 12, 2026 byYolly Del Prado


To sell a condo in Singapore, you will need to check whether Seller’s Stamp Duty applies, estimate your net sale proceeds, price and market the property, negotiate with buyers, grant an Option to Purchase and appoint a conveyancing lawyer to complete the transfer.


Unlike an HDB sale, there is no Minimum Occupation Period (MOP) or Intent to Sell requirement for a private condominium. You can sell at any time, although selling within the applicable holding period may result in Seller’s Stamp Duty.


Before putting up your listing, however, there are three numbers you should know: what your condo may sell for, the lowest offer you can reasonably accept and how much you may have left after the sale. They may sound similar, but they answer three very different questions.


---


## Condo Selling Process at a Glance


- 1. Check Whether Seller’s Stamp Duty Applies


- 2. Estimate How Much You May Have Left After Selling
- 3. Determine a Realistic Condo Selling Price
- 4. Decide Whether to Sell Independently or Engage an Agent
- 5. Prepare and Market Your Condo
- 6. Conduct Viewings and Evaluate Offers
- 7. Appoint a Lawyer and Grant the Option to Purchase
- 8. What Happens After the Buyer Exercises the OTP?
- 9. Complete the Sale and Hand Over the Condo
- How Long Does It Take to Sell a Condo in Singapore?
- What Does It Cost to Sell a Condo in Singapore?
- Should You Sell Your Condo Before Buying Your Next Home?
- Ready to Plan Your Condo Sale?
- Frequently Asked Questions About Selling a Condo


---


## 1. Check Whether Seller’s Stamp Duty Applies


You can sell a condo at any time in Singapore. However,[Seller’s Stamp Duty (SSD)](https://ohmyhome.com/en-sg/blog/seller-stamp-duty/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=backlink&utm_campaign=HowToSellCondo2026) may apply if you dispose of it within the SSD holding period that applies to its purchase date.


SSD is a tax, not a rule requiring you to live in the condo. It does not stop you from selling. Instead, it affects how much the sale may cost you.


### If You Purchased the Property From 11 March 2017 to 3 July 2025


**Holding period** **SSD rate**


Up to 1 year 12%


More than 1 year and up to 2 years 8%


More than 2 years and up to 3 years 4%


More than 3 years No SSD


### If You Purchased the Property on or After 4 July 2025


**Holding period** **SSD rate**


Up to 1 year 16%


More than 1 year and up to 2 years 12%


More than 2 years and up to 3 years 8%


More than 3 years and up to 4 years 4%


More than 4 years No SSD


SSD is calculated on the higher of the property’s selling price or market value. If it applies, it must generally be paid within 14 days from the date of the executed sale contract.


Acquisition dates before 11 March 2017 may be subject to different schedules, so check the latest IRAS Seller’s Stamp Duty rules or ask your lawyer to confirm the amount before you sell.


## 2. Estimate How Much You May Have Left After Selling


Your selling price is not the same as the amount you will receive in cash.


A simple starting point is:


**Estimated cash proceeds = Sale price − Outstanding loan − CPF refund − SSD, if applicable − Legal fees − Agent commission − Other selling costs**


The exact calculation depends on your circumstances, but the main deductions may include:


- Outstanding housing loan and applicable redemption costs
- CPF principal used for the property and accrued interest
- Seller’s Stamp Duty, if applicable
- Property-agent commission and GST
- Conveyancing fees
- Outstanding property tax or maintenance charges
- Agreed repairs, staging or moving costs


According to the CPF Board, sale proceeds for most private properties bought or refinanced on or after 1 September 2002 are generally used first to settle the outstanding housing loan, followed by the required CPF refund and other sale expenses such as legal fees.


If you used CPF savings to buy the condo, you will generally need to refund the principal amount withdrawn and accrued interest. You can check your estimated refund under the **“** ***What happens if*** **”** section of your CPF Home ownership dashboard. The money is returned to your CPF account rather than paid to the Government, and it may be available for another property purchase subject to CPF rules.


If the condo is sold at market value and the sale proceeds are insufficient after paying the outstanding housing loan, you generally do not need to top up the CPF shortfall in cash. However, option monies received in cash form part of the selling price and may need to be included in the refund.


You can read the full[CPF rules on refunds after selling a property](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/home-ownership/using-your-cpf-to-buy-a-home/cpf-refund-when-selling-or-transferring-property) before calculating your proceeds.


Alternatively, use HomerAI to[estimate your property value](https://ohmyhome.com/en-sg/homer-evaluation?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=clickthru&utm_campaign=HowToSellCondo2026) , CPF refund, outstanding loan and potential cash proceeds in one place.


## 3. Determine a Realistic Condo Selling Price


Your asking price should be based on recent comparable transactions, not simply the highest listing in your development.


Listings tell you what other owners hope to receive. Completed transactions show what buyers have actually agreed to pay.


Start by comparing units with similar characteristics:


- Development and location
- Floor area and layout
- Floor level
- Facing and view
- Tenure and remaining lease
- Renovation condition
- Balcony, private enclosed space (PES) area or roof terrace area
- Proximity to transport, schools and amenities
- Transaction date


The closer the comparison, the more useful it becomes. A high-floor renovated unit with an open view may not be directly comparable to a lower-floor unit facing a road, even if both have the same number of bedrooms.


You can review recorded private residential transactions through URA’s Property Data e-services and use[HomerAI’s free condo valuation tool](https://ohmyhome.com/en-sg/homer/condo-valuation?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=clickthru&utm_campaign=HowToSellCondo2026) for an estimated sale and rental value, nearby transactions and historical price trends.


An automated estimate is a useful starting point, but it cannot fully assess your unit’s condition, view, facing or buyer demand at that particular moment. That is where an on-site assessment and project-specific transaction analysis can add context.


## 4. Decide Whether to Sell Independently or Engage an Agent


You are not legally required to appoint a property agent to sell a condo in Singapore. You may market the property, conduct viewings and negotiate directly with buyers yourself.


However, you will still need a conveyancing lawyer to handle the legal transfer.


If you[engage a property agent](https://ohmyhome.com/en-sg/property-agent-services/book-an-agent/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=clickthru&utm_campaign=HowToSellCondo2026) , the agent can assist with:


- Reviewing comparable transactions
- Advising on the asking price
- Preparing the listing and marketing plan
- Advertising the unit
- Coordinating enquiries and viewings
- Communicating offers and counter-offers
- Negotiating terms
- Coordinating with the buyer’s agent and lawyers
- Keeping the transaction moving towards completion


The Council for Estate Agencies does not prescribe a fixed commission rate. You should negotiate the fee, clarify whether GST applies and record the agreed terms in the Prescribed Estate Agency Agreement.


You should also[verify the agent’s registration and transaction history](https://ohmyhome.com/en-sg/blog/how-to-check-property-agent-transaction-record-in-cea-public-register/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=backlink&utm_campaign=HowToSellCondo2026) through the CEA Public Register.


The agency’s reputation matters, but the individual agent handling your property is just as important. Ask prospective agents about recent transactions in your development or genuinely comparable projects, who will conduct the viewings and how they arrived at their recommended price.


## 5. Prepare and Market Your Condo


You do not necessarily need an expensive renovation before selling. In many cases, decluttering, deep cleaning, completing small repairs and presenting each room properly can make a greater difference than undertaking major works you may not recover through the sale.


Before photographing or showing the property:


- Remove unnecessary furniture and personal items
- Repair visibly damaged fixtures
- Replace faulty lights
- Clean windows, floors, bathrooms and kitchen surfaces
- Let in natural light where possible
- Prepare an accurate inventory of items included in the sale
- Gather information buyers may ask for, such as maintenance fees and approved alterations


Your listing should describe the property accurately. Avoid exaggerated claims about floor area, tenure, school eligibility or future developments that cannot be verified.


[A good marketing plan](https://ohmyhome.com/en-sg/blog/5-expert-tactics-to-market-your-property-listing-like-a-pro/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=backlink&utm_campaign=HowToSellCondo2026) should also identify the unit’s likely buyer instead of presenting it as suitable for everyone. A compact city-fringe condo may appeal to a different buyer from a large family unit near schools, while an investment property with an existing tenancy requires another approach altogether.


## 6. Conduct Viewings and Evaluate Offers


The highest offer is attractive, but price is not the only term worth reviewing.


Before accepting, consider:


- The proposed purchase price
- The buyer’s financing position
- The requested option period
- The proposed completion date
- Whether vacant possession is required
- Whether the property is sold with an existing tenancy
- Furniture, appliances or fixtures included in the sale
- Any special conditions attached to the offer


This becomes particularly important if you are also buying another home. An offer that fits the timeline for your next property may be more workable than a slightly higher offer with terms that leave you paying for temporary accommodation or carrying two properties longer than planned.


Before agreeing to a price, return to your net-proceeds calculation. A headline offer is only useful if the resulting funds are enough for your next step.


## 7. Appoint a Lawyer and Grant the Option to Purchase


Once you are ready to accept an offer,[engage a conveyancing lawyer](https://ohmyhome.com/en-sg/home-services/legal-conveyancing/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=clickthru&utm_campaign=HowToSellCondo2026) if you have not already done so.


The lawyer can help prepare or review the Option to Purchase (OTP), conduct the conveyancing work, redeem the existing mortgage, arrange the CPF refund and complete the legal transfer.


CEA provides an Option to Purchase template for private residential property, although its use is not compulsory and the parties may negotiate or amend the terms.


The OTP should clearly state:


- The agreed purchase price
- The option money
- The deadline for the buyer to exercise the option
- The balance deposit payable upon exercise
- The scheduled completion date
- Whether vacant possession will be provided
- Any tenancy or inventory included
- Other conditions agreed between the parties


A common private-resale arrangement involves the buyer paying 1% of the purchase price as option money and a further 4% when exercising the OTP. However, these are customary figures rather than universal statutory amounts. The signed OTP determines the actual fees and deadlines.


CEA’s standard template provides for an option period ending on a stated date or before the expiry of two weeks from the option date. However, parties may negotiate different terms, so do not assume every private-property OTP follows the same timeframe.


Once granted, the OTP gives the buyer the right to purchase the condo according to its terms. If the buyer does not exercise it before the deadline, the option will generally lapse and the option money may be forfeited, subject to the contract.


## 8. What Happens After the Buyer Exercises the OTP?


Once the buyer validly exercises the OTP and pays the required deposit, a binding agreement for the sale and purchase of the property is formed.


The conveyancing lawyers will then handle matters such as:


- Legal requisitions and title checks
- Redemption of the seller’s outstanding mortgage
- Discharge of any CPF charge
- Required CPF refund
- Seller’s Stamp Duty, if applicable
- Property-tax apportionment
- Preparation and execution of transfer documents
- Collection and distribution of the sale proceeds


Property tax is payable annually in advance. During the sale, the buyer may reimburse you for the portion covering the period after completion. This apportionment is a private arrangement that the lawyers will usually calculate. You should also settle outstanding property tax and check when to terminate any related GIRO arrangement.


If you are selling with an existing tenancy, the sale documents should clearly state whether the buyer will take over the property subject to the existing tenancy. The tenancy documents, deposit and handover arrangements should be addressed during conveyancing.


## 9. Complete the Sale and Hand Over the Condo


On the scheduled completion date, the buyer pays the remaining purchase price through the conveyancing process and legal ownership is transferred.


Your lawyer will apply the sale proceeds towards the relevant payments, including the outstanding mortgage, CPF refund and transaction expenses. The remaining amount is then released to you according to the completion arrangements.


Before handing over the property:


- Remove your belongings unless they are included in the sale
- Settle outstanding maintenance contributions
- Provide the agreed keys, access cards and remotes
- Record meter readings where necessary
- Follow the agreed vacant-possession or tenancy arrangements
- Keep copies of the completed transaction documents


If you need to remain in the property after completion, do not assume this will be allowed automatically. Any post-completion stay should be negotiated in advance and documented properly with legal advice.


## How Long Does It Take to Sell a Condo in Singapore?


There is no fixed total timeline because finding a buyer may take days or several months, depending on the property, asking price and market demand.


Once an OTP is granted, the buyer must exercise it within the period stated in the document. CEA’s standard template provides for a specified expiry date or, where applicable, an option period of two weeks. The scheduled legal completion date is also stated in the OTP and may be changed by agreement between the parties.


Therefore, it is better to plan the sale in separate stages:


**Stage** **What affects the timing**


Preparation and listing Valuation, photography, repairs and marketing


Finding a buyer Price, demand, competition and viewing response


OTP period Deadline agreed in the OTP


Conveyancing and completion Contractual completion date, financing and legal work


If you are buying another home, base your plans on the agreed completion date rather than the date you first list the condo.

## What Does It Cost to Sell a Condo in Singapore?


Your costs may include:


**Cost** **When it may apply**


Seller’s Stamp Duty If sold within the applicable SSD holding period


Property-agent commission If you engage an agent


GST on commission If charged by a GST-registered property agency


Conveyancing fees For the legal transfer and related work


Mortgage redemption costs If an existing housing loan must be settled


CPF refund If CPF savings were used for the property


Property tax and maintenance charges Outstanding amounts and any apportionment made upon completion


Repairs, cleaning or staging Depending on the unit’s condition and marketing plan


Moving or temporary accommodation Depending on your next-home timeline


The CPF refund is not a transaction fee, but it reduces the amount of sale proceeds immediately available in cash. This is why it should still be included in your planning.


## Should You Sell Your Condo Before Buying Your Next Home?


Selling first usually tells you exactly how much money is available for the next purchase and can reduce the risk of carrying two properties at once. However, you may need temporary accommodation if your next home is not ready.


Buying first gives you more certainty over where you will move, but it may require more available cash, bridging arrangements or the ability to carry overlapping financial commitments. It may also affect the Additional Buyer’s Stamp Duty payable on the next property, depending on your ownership profile and eligibility for any remission.


The better order depends on your finances, family needs, next-property type and timing. Work through the numbers before choosing based on convenience alone.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Selling a Condo


### Can I sell my condo at any time?


Yes. There is no HDB-style MOP for a private condo. However, Seller’s Stamp Duty may apply if you sell within the relevant holding period, depending on when you purchased the property.


### Do I need a property agent to sell my condo?


No. You may market and negotiate the sale yourself, although you will still need a conveyancing lawyer for the legal transfer. If you appoint an agent, agree on the commission and scope of work in writing before marketing begins.


### How much CPF must I refund after selling my condo?


You will generally need to refund the CPF principal used for the property and accrued interest. The exact amount can be checked through the “ *What happens if* ” section of your CPF Home ownership dashboard. Different rules may apply in certain circumstances, including for some owners aged 55 or above.
